overview:
Knowledge‑obscuring karma (jñānāvaraṇīya‑karma) is one of the eight primary categories of karma described in Jain philosophy, classified within the four destructive (ghātiyā) karmas. Its defining function is to obstruct the soul’s innate capacity for **jñāna**, the pure, limitless knowledge that is an inherent attribute of every jīva. In Jain metaphysics, the soul is naturally endowed with perfect knowledge, perception, bliss, and energy. However, due to the influx (āsrava) and binding (bandha) of karmic matter, these qualities become partially or fully obscured. Jñānāvaraṇīya‑karma specifically veils knowledge, preventing the soul from experiencing its true omniscient state.

Jain texts identify **five types of knowledge**—mati (sensory‑mental cognition), śruta (scriptural knowledge), avadhi (clairvoyance), manaḥparyāya (telepathy), and kevala‑jñāna (omniscience). Knowledge‑obscuring karma can obstruct each of these in different degrees. The obstruction is not conceptual or psychological but metaphysical: subtle karmic particles bind to the soul and limit its cognitive radiance. As these karmas are gradually shed through right conduct, austerities, and the progressive purification described in the fourteen guṇasthānas, the soul’s knowledge becomes increasingly unobstructed.

In Jain cosmology, the complete destruction (kṣaya) of jñānāvaraṇīya‑karma occurs only at the **12th guṇasthāna**, immediately preceding omniscience. When this karma is fully eliminated, the soul attains kevala‑jñāna, an infinite and direct knowledge of all substances and their modes across past, present, and future. The tradition emphasizes that this state is not acquired but uncovered—the soul always possesses perfect knowledge, and karma merely obscures it.

Different Jain traditions—Digambara, Śvetāmbara Mūrti‑pūjaka, Sthānakavāsī, and Terāpanth—agree on the fundamental nature of jñānāvaraṇīya‑karma, though their commentarial literature may differ in technical classifications, examples, and metaphysical elaboration. Across traditions, this karma is considered central to understanding bondage, liberation, and the path of spiritual purification.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.notes: Tattvārtha Sūtra 8.5 identifies jñānāvaraṇīya‑karma as one of the ghātiyā karmas. Subsequent sūtras classify the five types of knowledge and explain how karma obstructs each. This text is accepted across Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions, though commentaries differ.

primary_sources.title: Gommatasāra (Karmakāṇḍa)
primary_sources.author: Nemicandra Siddhānta‑cakravartin
primary_sources.original_text: पञ्चविदं ज्ञानं तं अवरन्ति एत्थं अवरणियं
primary_sources.transliteration: pañcavidaṃ jñānaṃ taṃ avaranti etthaṃ avaraṇiyaṃ
primary_sources.translation: “That which obstructs the five kinds of knowledge is called knowledge‑obscuring karma.”
primary_sources.notes: A Digambara technical treatise detailing karmic categories, their binding conditions, and their destruction. Provides extensive analysis of how jñānāvaraṇīya‑karma affects clairvoyance and omniscience.

primary_sources.title: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Śvetāmbara canonical text
primary_sources.notes: Used in Śvetāmbara traditions to illustrate how karmic veiling prevents the emergence of true cognition. Commentaries emphasize ethical causes of karmic influx.

misconceptions.myth: Knowledge‑obscuring karma means that the soul lacks knowledge until it learns or acquires it.
misconceptions.reality: Jain philosophy teaches that the soul inherently possesses infinite knowledge; karma only veils it. Spiritual practice removes the obstruction rather than adding new knowledge.

misconceptions.myth: Knowledge‑obscuring karma only affects scriptural or intellectual learning.
misconceptions.reality: It obstructs all five types of knowledge, including clairvoyance and omniscience. Its scope is metaphysical, not limited to intellectual capacity.

misconceptions.myth: Once knowledge‑obscuring karma is reduced, omniscience is easily attained.
misconceptions.reality: Complete destruction of this karma occurs only at advanced guṇasthānas and requires simultaneous elimination of other destructive karmas. It is a rare and highly elevated spiritual state.
